extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students (patent litigation practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the proof and evidentiary standards for defenses (license, statute of limitations, estoppel, release, res judicata) and on the legal rules and evidence for measuring damages in patent infringement suits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plea of license must be proved by showing actual grant
rubrics_metrics.description: A plea of license must be sustained by proof that a license was actually granted; negotiations alone do not prove an actual license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If proved as a completed contract, a plea of license ends the case. An oral license may be proved by any proper testimony. When an absolute written license is produced by the defendant, the burden shifts to the plaintiff to show it was delivered as an escrow. A license given as part of a settlement of a suit is not evidence against a stranger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional license requires performance of conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a license is conditional, the defendant must perform the conditions, and if justifying under the license must show the conditions were performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant who relies on a conditional license must prove the facts establishing its creation and satisfaction; failure to perform the conditions defeats the license defence (cases: Brooks v. Stolley, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied licenses arise from facts (sale, express grant, practicality)
rubrics_metrics.description: A license to make may be implied from an express license to use or sell when those rights cannot reasonably be enjoyed without the right to make; conversely, a license to use or sell may be implied from an express license to make in like manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sale of a specific article without restrictions by one with authority under the patent may imply a license to use/sell it. Sale by owner of a device whose sole utility is in a process may give a license to employ that process. The nature and sources of evidence for an implied license are suggested by the facts from which the license is implied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope-of-license proof: acts must be within conferred authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant relying on a license must show that his acts were performed under the authority conferred and not in antagonism to the patent or under a license from a different patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If acts exceed the license's scope the licensee is an infringer; plaintiff must rebut claims of authority by denying existence or by counter evidence, or by showing defendant's acts fall outside conferred authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express license to make may carry use/sell rights (and vice versa)
rubrics_metrics.description: An express license to make may carry the right to use or sell; likewise an express license to use or sell may carry the right to make in appropriate circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See cross-references (sections cited §§ 811, 812, 818). A lawful sale without restrictions carries the right to use and sometimes to sell; purchaser of a machine from the patentee may defend on ground of license to use machine and process together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof when claiming license arises from another patent
rubrics_metrics.description: No evidence that the defendant is licensee or owner under a different patent excuses infringement which appears from comparing devices with the plaintiff's patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant must show privity and authority under the asserted patent; mere assertion of license under a different patent is insufficient if comparison shows infringement of plaintiff's patent (cases: Blanchard v. Putnam, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of limitations defence must be specially pleaded; burden on defendant
rubrics_metrics.description: The twenty-second defence (statute of limitations) must be specially pleaded and the burden of proof on the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nature of evidence depends on when the limitations period begins (date of infringement vs. expiration of patent). If statute begins at patent expiration, proof comes from patent instrument statements, surrender/repeal records, or evidence of prior patents limiting term. Exceptions in statute require corresponding evidence on both sides. Testimony about acts of infringement and record date of institution shows whether suit commenced within prescribed time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel defence requirements and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Twenty-third defence (estoppel) is asserted by defendant and carries the burden of proof; written instruments must clearly show statements creating estoppel and privity when parties are not signatories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estoppel in pais is implied from plaintiff's actions or omissions; defendant must prove the circumstances and his reliance thereon as guiding his conduct. Evidence must be tailored to alleged facts (e.g., unstamped articles shown in market to support estoppel for failure to stamp). Plaintiff may rebut by proving actual notice before infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Release defence: production and proof of release
rubrics_metrics.description: The twenty-fourth defence (release) asserts the cause of action has been released by the plaintiff; burden of proof is on defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When release is in writing it must be produced or absence explained and its contents proved. If release is part of a broader transaction, enough of the transaction must be proved to show plaintiff intended the release and that it was made on lawful consideration. Reasonable doubt as to existence or applicability of release favors the plaintiff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Res judicata (merger, estoppel by prior judgment) defence standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The twenty-fifth defence asserts the cause has been extinguished by or merged in a judgment; defendant bears the burden of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence must show the same acts were the subject of a prior suit with a judgment rendered for the defendant on a point fatal to the cause of action, or for the plaintiff for damages. A record or certified copy of the judgment must be offered, plus other evidence to connect parties or show privity (judgment estops only when record shows the particular point was heard and decided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Five averments of declaration and special evidence rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration averments include (1) invention by patentee/assignor, (2) lawful issue and existence of patent, (3) title of plaintiff, (4) infringement by defendant, and (5) that infringement resulted in damage; special rules of evidence apply to the first four; the fifth requires separate principles for damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first four averments have discussed special evidentiary rules; evidence admissible on damages (the fifth averment) depends on principles of damages which are distinct and must be considered separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between equity and law measures of recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a fundamental distinction: at law the remedy is compensatory damages for injury sustained; in equity the remedy is accounting for gains and profits (defendant treated as trustee) and, if necessary, additional relief to redress injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity and law impose different obligations and use different standards for estimating monetary relief; gains and profits (equity) are distinct from damages (law) and courts must not import doctrines from one to the other without confusion. Historic election of remedies has been altered by statute (post-1870) so the distinctions remain material for how recovery is measured and what evidence is admissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between rule of damages and rules of evidence concerning damages
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule of damages (nominal vs actual) is fixed; the rules of evidence about proving amount vary widely and must suit the specific facts of each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages law recognizes nominal and actual damages and when each is appropriate, but evidence admissibility and weight vary because infringement may inflict injuries of varied degrees/characters; thus no single evidentiary prescription fits all patent cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of nominal damages
rubrics_metrics.description: When jury finds for plaintiff on the first four averments, they must award at least nominal damages; law implies damage from violation even if infringement was innocent or caused no particular injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If plaintiff cannot prove amount of actual damages, nominal damages within ordinary limits should be given (examples: six cents affirmed in some cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of actual damages (legal measure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual damages are compensatory — indemnity for injury inflicted; measured by the direct and immediate consequences to the plaintiff from the date of infringement to institution of the suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of existence and extent of consequences must be clear and definite to enable jury estimation; absent such proof (through plaintiff's fault or misfortune) only nominal damages can be awarded. Vindictive or exemplary damages are not permitted as a rule, though courts have power to increase awards in cases of malicious or persistent injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence for damages varies with how patentee exploits monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules of evidence concerning damages depend on the method by which the plaintiff receives benefits of the monopoly and how those benefits are affected by the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If patentee derives no advantage from the rights, damages should be graduately limited to compensate the plaintiff only for the injury done. In aggravated cases (circumstances calling for vindictive damages), damages may be adjusted accordingly, but must reflect compensation for actual injury normally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual damages: limitations and illustrative rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Various subsidiary rules govern actual damages: only direct and immediate damages recoverable; remote/consequential damages generally not recoverable; verdict covers damages up to date of writ; plaintiff must affirmatively prove amount; proof sometimes may use license price as guide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury may estimate damages from general evidence for the period of infringement up to the writ but not for the whole term of the patent. Good faith of defendant is not an absolute excuse. Examples and citations outline situations (e.g., medicines or trivial per-unit value inventions where license price may guide damage calculation; six-cent nominal damages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable accounting (profits) principles
rubrics_metrics.description: In equity the plaintiff may recover the profits the defendant made by unlawful use as if the defendant were a trustee; if defendant made no profit there may be no recovery on an accounting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If defendant used the invention so unskillfully that he realized no profit, there could be no recovery in equity; conversely, where defendant profits, plaintiff may recover gains and profits (and possibly damages in addition if injury exceeds profits in equity actions).
